newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ political parties hit the campaign trail.
newsitem.headline: NZ political parties hit the campaign trail.

text.p: Two parties from almost opposite ends of the political spectrum converged on Auckland on Sunday to kick off their campaigns for New Zealand's October 12 general election.
At one end, the main opposition Labour Party launched a slick multi-cultural campaign in downtown Auckland which was aimed at the underprivileged.
At the other, political minnow Act New Zealand was targeting middle-income New Zealand in the well-off suburb of Epsom.

Labour Leader Helen Clark, whose party has struggled to overcome the memories of the reformist Labour government of 1984-90, made a pitch to the underpaid, the unions, the indigenous Maori and Pacific Islanders.
She promised a return to a more supportive government in the key areas of education, health and welfare.

In a presentation steeped in history, Clark made little mention of 1984-90, an administration that angered Labour's support base by embarking on a programme of wide-ranging economic reform, deregulation and privatisation.
When Labour was toppled by Prime Minister Jim Bolger's National Party in 1990, National continued the economic reform process with missionary zeal.
Clark asked what that had done to the quality of the state's free health care system. "That has all been destroyed by people who know the costs of everything and the value of nothing."
Teachers, social workers, nurses and the police were under strain as they bore the brunt of an "increasingly aggressive and abusive underclass".
The election will be the first to be held under the new, German-style Mixed Member Proportional (MMP) electoral system, which is expected to deliver coalition governments.
Clark accused the governing National Party of listening only to big business and she firmly ruled out any alliance with Labour's conservative rival.
Across town at Epsom, Act New Zealand Leader Richard Prebble was extolling the virtues of individual responsibility and freedom to an enthusiastic crowd of around 1,200.
Under MMP, voters will get two votes, one for their electorate and one for a party list. Parties need to garner support of more than five percent to secure a "list" seat.
Prebble, a key member of the 1984-90 Labour government, told supporters that Act would cross the threshold from its current rating of four percent.
He also reiterated the party's commitment to a flat tax rate, removal of taxes on employer-sponsored health insurance, a compulsory pension scheme and an open economy.
A recent opinion poll said National had 38 percent support, Labour 21 percent, economic nationalist NZ First 18 percent and the left-wing Alliance Party 12 percent.
